entry.title: AI Agent Costs: Metrics Beyond Token Count
entry.summary: Token price is easy to quote, but it is not the same as the cost of a useful completed task. An agent may spend tokens on retries, calls, retrieval, orchestration, and human correction. Teams that optimize only the model bill can miss the expensive parts of the workflow. Track total cost per successful task, not just per request. Include model usage, search or database calls, tool execution, infrastructure, and review time. Separate successful runs from failed or abandoned ones so a cheap failure does not look like an efficiency win. Break down spend by workflow, step, model, and outcome. Watch for repeated tool calls, oversized context, unnecessary reasoning passes, and retrieval that returns too much material. Pair cost with quality, latency, and escalation rate. A smaller model may reduce inference expense but increase retries or human review. A larger model may be justified for a narrow high-risk decision while a simpler model handles classification or routing. Test the tradeoff with representative tasks. Set a maximum step count, retry policy, timeout, and cost threshold. Define a safe fallback when a run approaches its budget. Alert on changes in cost per successful outcome, then investigate the workflow change behind them. Cost governance is a product decision: know what outcome you are buying and what quality level is acceptable. I write about practical AI delivery at https://umer-amin.vercel.app/. Which cost do you track today: tokens, completed task, or human time?

entry.title: A Practical Incident Runbook for AI Workflows
entry.summary: When an AI workflow breaks, responders need to know what it tried to do and which actions may already have happened. A useful incident runbook should help contain the issue first, then preserve evidence and restore service safely. Disable the affected trigger or tool permission if the agent could repeat a harmful action. Pause queued jobs when duplicate execution is possible. Keep a human path available for urgent requests. Record the first known failure time, workflow version, model and prompt changes, affected integrations, and example run IDs. Check whether the issue is a bad answer, tool failure, latency spike, or unintended external change. Avoid copying sensitive prompts or user data into broad incident channels. Use a known-good workflow or manual process while investigating. If external writes occurred, reconcile them with the system of record before replaying jobs. Do not blindly retry a non-idempotent action. Test the fix against the failed case and nearby edge cases. Re-enable traffic gradually, watch the completion and error signals, and document who owns the next step. Turn the incident into an evaluation case, alert, or permission boundary. The runbook should name an incident lead, a technical owner, rollback criteria, and customer communication owner. Keep it short enough to use under pressure and review it after changes to tools or workflows. More notes on operational AI delivery: https://umer-amin.vercel.app/. What is the first action your team takes when an agent starts behaving unpredictably?

entry.summary: Hey guys! 👋🏻 I wanted to share a good security fix I applied to my microforum, Axion. It's about stopping attackers from finding out which usernames exist through timing attacks. entry.title: AI Agent Evaluation: How to Test Workflows That Change Their Answers
entry.summary: Traditional tests expect the same input to produce the same output. AI workflows can vary, so testing only exact text matches creates brittle suites—or false confidence when the expected phrase appears but the task failed. For each workflow, write the user goal, allowed actions, required evidence, and unacceptable outcomes. A support agent might need to answer from approved policy, cite the relevant source, and ask for help when the source is missing. Those conditions matter more than whether it uses a particular sentence. Collect realistic requests, edge cases, ambiguous inputs, and known failure examples. Include cases with missing context, conflicting instructions, malformed data, and tool errors. Keep a stable test set for regressions and a separate fresh set for discovering new problems. Score multiple dimensions: task completion, factual grounding, tool selection, policy adherence, escalation behavior, latency, and cost. Use deterministic checks where possible. For open-ended quality, use human review or a calibrated judge, then manually inspect disagreements. Run evaluations across prompt, model, retrieval, and tool changes. Include the whole path: input preparation, permissions, retries, side effects, and final handoff. A model can improve its answer while the workflow becomes less safe. Set release thresholds for critical behaviors. If a change drops a safety or task metric, stop rollout or send it to a limited test group. Track production feedback and turn incidents into new evaluation cases. Good evaluation is a loop: define success, test representative cases, review failures, and improve the system. It makes model variation measurable instead of mysterious. I share practical AI delivery notes at https://umer-amin.vercel.app/. How are you testing behavior when there is no single “correct” sentence?

entry.title: The AI Verification Gap: Review AI Code Without Rubber-Stamping It
entry.summary: AI can produce a patch that looks tidy and still violates an assumption nobody wrote down. The risk is not simply that generated code contains bugs. It is that reviewers become less critical when the diff arrives quickly and reads confidently. Before reading line by line, restate the expected behavior and the boundary of the change. Which user-visible outcome should improve? Which existing behavior must stay the same? What should happen when input is missing, invalid, slow, or repeated? Then inspect the diff for hidden scope: new dependencies, permission changes, network calls, data handling, migrations, and fallback behavior. Ask the model to explain the assumptions it used, but verify those assumptions against the codebase and product requirements. Run focused tests, then inspect what they do not cover. Add a regression test for the original failure, and exercise boundary cases. For infrastructure or automation changes, verify the plan, permissions, rollback, and observable success signal. A green test suite is evidence, not proof that every risk is gone. Ask for a second pass that looks for security, failure paths, and unintended behavior. Treat its findings as hypotheses to check. Keep a human accountable for accepting the change, especially when it can modify data, grant access, or affect production. A small review checklist helps: intent, assumptions, tests, security, operations, rollback, and ownership. The goal is not to slow every patch; it is to make the important questions repeatable. entry.title: AI Agent Observability: What to Log Before Production
entry.summary: AI agents can fail in ways a normal application log will not explain. A workflow may call the wrong tool, act on stale context, repeat a step, or return a polished answer that hides a broken handoff. If you only log the final response, debugging becomes guesswork. For each run, capture a run ID, timestamp, workflow and prompt version, model and tool names, and the outcome. Record each meaningful step: what input the agent received, which tool it selected, whether the tool succeeded, and what happened next. Redact secrets and personal data before storing anything. Keep the trace structured. A useful event might include run_id, step_id, tool, status, duration_ms, and an error category. Keep full prompts and outputs only when your retention policy and user expectations allow it. Track task completion, retries, tool errors, timeouts, human escalations, and latency. Separate model errors from integration errors. A rising retry rate can be an early warning even while the service still reports healthy. Add alerts for actionable conditions: repeated tool failure, unusual run duration, failed handoff, or a drop in verified completion. Avoid alerting on every model variation; route useful signals to the people who can respond. A trace should let an operator answer: what did the agent try, what evidence did it use, what changed, and where did it stop? Include links between the user request, workflow run, tool calls, and resulting system action. Start with one critical workflow. Define what success means, instrument each decision and external action, then test a deliberately failing dependency. Observability is useful when the team can detect, explain, and safely recover from a bad run. I’m documenting practical AI delivery and technical project management at https://umer-amin.vercel.app/. entry.title: USPTO's own trademark APIs now all require a key — the keyless answer is a different office's database
entry.summary:
If you want to check whether a name is already a registered US trademark, the obvious place to look is the USPTO's own systems. As of October 2026, every official route we could find now requires an API key — and the keyless answer to "is this a US trademark" turns out to live on a server EUIPO runs, not USPTO. TSDR (tsdrapi.uspto.gov), the status-and-document API wrapper docs usually point to first, now returns 401 — but not a JSON error. The body is plain text: HTTP/1.1 401 Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8
Beginning October 2, you'll need to register for an API key to download bulk data from our TSDR APIs. Register for an API key at https://account.uspto.gov/api-manager/.
